newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japanese pop singer is fashion phenomenon.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japanese pop singer is fashion phenomenon.

text.p: Tokyo's most fashionable districts are being overrun by tanned, teenage girls with tight, short T-shirts, long dyed brown hair, thin eyebrows, mini-skirts and long boots.

Dubbed "Amuraa", they are virtual clones of Japan's latest pop phenomenon, 18-year-old Namie Amuro, who has taken the Japanese music scene by storm. Her songs are widely sung and her dance steps are copied in karaoke rooms around Japan.
The word Amuraa has entered the language and alludes to another widely-used term -- "Shanelaa" -- meaning a woman favouring items from the French fashion house Chanel.

Amuro -- also seen as a teen fashion guru -- has sold more than three million copies of her new album "Sweet 19 Blues", released in late July. She has also sold about six million CD singles in the past year.
Her baby face and petite appearance feature in television commercials, variety shows and music programmes almost daily. She starred in her first film this summer.
But Amuro says she enjoys singing the most.

"I like singing live on stage. That's what I enjoy the most ... more than anything else," Amuro, who turns 19 on September 20, told Reuters in an interview. "I want to dance and sing funky music as much as I can.
"I still can't feel this (Amuraa) phenomenon is about me. I've only noticed the trend through television," she said.
The flamboyant singer has just completed a final leg of her summer tour in which the final two concerts attracted 60,000 fans to a seaside stadium near Tokyo.
Backed by all non-Japanese musicians, Amuro sang and danced through 20 of her hits, mostly techno beat dance music. Many of her fans sang and danced along throughout the show.
The last song of the show and the album title track "Sweet 19 Blues" describe her unease about being popular.

"I have to constantly care about how I look in public ... like when I'm walking in the street," she said. "I have to be extra sensitive to look good on television, but it's not easy doing that all the time. I sometimes feel lonesome too."

A female teenage singer commonly attracts a mainly male audience in Japan, but for Amuro it is different: in Tokyo more than half of the audience were women, many dressed in imitation of her "Amuraa" style.

One 18-year old high-school girl proudly showed off her small brown T-shirt with a small brand logo on. "I bought this T-shirt after seeing her wear this at a concert in May. I bought this especially for this occasion."
In the interview, Amuro was dressed in light brown summer knitted sweater over a black T-shirt, with black cotton mini-skirt, black socks and her symbol black short boots.
Husky-voiced Amuro says she prefers to dress casually in private. "I'm usually dressed like this."
Amuro is one of the few Japanese artists who can pack a stadium, but her success did not come overnight after she left her home-town in remote Okinawa island five years ago.
She described bitterly the experience of performing in a supermarket where no one was listening.
"Customers were busy shopping," she said. "But the sad part was that I noticed that workers at the supermarket were trying to be nice by pretending to listen."
Amuro is expected to be one of the biggest selling recording artists this year, but success has not spoiled her.
"People around me have changed, but my lifestyle has not actually changed much. I'm still not interested in spending money on luxury brand items," the Okinawan singer said.
"Of course I want go out with people my age, but more than that I enjoy working and that's what I want to do the most now."
